lines.say: Your orders page takes nine seconds to load. To show you ten orders, your app asks the database for a million.
lines.show: Your orders page takes *nine seconds* to load. To show you *ten orders,* your app asks the database for [a million.]

lines.say: Your database keeps orders like a giant spreadsheet: one row per order, from every user, and a column for each detail. Your app's request says: send me all of it.
lines.show: Your database keeps orders like a giant *spreadsheet:* one row per order, from *every user,* and a column for each detail. Your app's request says: [send me all of it.]

lines.say: A million rows, with every column, travel to your app. Your code keeps your ten newest, and throws the rest away.
lines.show: *A million rows,* with every column, travel to your app. Your code keeps your *ten newest,* and [throws the rest away.]

lines.say: That request is called a query. A better one asks for exactly what the page shows: your ten newest orders, with just the details on screen.
lines.show: That request is called a *query.* A better one asks for exactly what the page shows: [your ten newest orders,] with just the details on screen.

lines.say: Like a shopping list: you ask for milk and eggs, not the whole shop delivered to your door.
lines.show: Like a *shopping list:* you ask for milk and eggs, not [the whole shop] delivered to your door.

lines.say: That's one part of query optimization: ten rows come back instead of a million, so there's far less to send and process.
lines.show: That's one part of [query optimization:] *ten rows* come back instead of a million, so there's far less to send and *process.*

lines.say: To see how the database finds those rows, put EXPLAIN in front of the query. If it reads the whole table just to find a few rows, an index can help.
lines.show: To see how the database finds those rows, put [EXPLAIN] in front of the query. If it reads the *whole table* just to find a few rows, an *index* can help.
